register.name: South Carolina General Assembly - South Carolina Code of Laws (South Carolina Legislative Council / Legislative Services Agency)
register.access_notes: Fully accessible. Plain HTTPS GET with the honest user agent 'canon-legislation-indexer/1.0 (legalese/canon corpus metadata survey)' worked with no challenge, no CAPTCHA and no block. Structure: /code/statmast.php is the master index of the 63 Titles with the Legislative Council's disclaimer and currency statement; /code/titleNN.php is a per-title chapter index; /code/tNNcCCC.php is a per-chapter page (note the zero padding - Title 8 Chapter 11 is /code/t08c011.php, Title 41 Chapter 10 is /code/t41c010.php). Chapter pages carry the full statutory text, so only the chapter heading, article headings, section numbers, section catchlines and HISTORY effective-date lines were read and recorded; the downloaded copies of the larger chapter pages were deleted immediately after the headings were extracted, and no statute text was copied into this record. The site sits behind Cloudflare: 2 of about 22 requests returned a transient HTTP 522 (origin timeout) and succeeded on a single retry after a pause; this is a flaky origin, not a block. About 22 requests in total, spaced 2 s apart. Verification used only the register's own index, title, chapter and disclaimer pages.

licence.summary: Open for the statutory text, by the register's own express permission. The Legislative Council's disclaimer at the head of the Code of Laws index grants copying of the Code text, numbering, history and the Effect of Amendment, Editor's and Code Commissioner's notes from the website without permission and without fee. There is no copyright notice anywhere on the Code pages. That express permission sits on top of the constitutional position: under the government edicts doctrine confirmed in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020), the text, numbering and section catchlines of the South Carolina Code, being the work of legislators acting in their legislative capacity, are outside copyright altogether, so reuse and adaptation are lawful regardless. Two qualifications a human should note. First, the site-wide disclaimer at https://www.scstatehouse.gov/disclaimer.php says of the General Assembly website generally that 'This information is intended for personal, not commercial, uses.' - a broad website-wide statement that sits awkwardly with the Code-specific permission; the Code-specific and more particular permission should govern for the Code text, and in any event the doctrine means the text cannot be restricted by either statement. Second, the website version is expressly not the official version: the printed South Carolina Code of Laws Annotated is, and the annotations in that commercial edition (published by LexisNexis) are not part of what the permission covers and are not part of the enacted text. Treated as open: reuse and adaptation permitted.
licence.attribution: none required; good practice is to cite 'South Carolina Code of Laws' with the title, chapter and the 'current through the 2025 Session' currency statement, and not to present a copy as the official version
licence.quote: The South Carolina Code, consisting only of Code text, numbering, history, and Effect of Amendment, Editor's, and Code Commissioner's notes may be copied from this website at the reader's expense and effort without need for permission.

topic_gaps.reason: No South Carolina statute governs termination of employment or severance pay. South Carolina is an at-will state and the exceptions are common-law (public policy; handbook-based contract). The only statutory rule on separation is sec. 41-10-50 in the Payment of Wages chapter, requiring final wages to be paid within 48 hours of discharge or by the next regular payday: that is a wage-payment duty, not a termination statute, and it is already captured under Payroll/wages. Collective redundancy notice is federal (WARN Act, 29 U.S.C. ch. 23); there is no South Carolina mini-WARN Act. Verified by reading the Title 41 chapter index at https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/title41.php, on which no chapter deals with termination or severance.

No state statute. Compensation for denied boarding, delay and cancellation is federal: 14 C.F.R. part 250 and 49 U.S.C. ch. 417 for air, 49 U.S.C. for rail. Title 58's carrier chapters (ch. 58-13 Carriers Generally, ch. 58-23 Motor Vehicle Carriers, ch. 58-25 Regional Transportation Authority Law), verified on https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/title58.php, regulate carriers for safety, franchising and rates and create no passenger compensation entitlement.
Federal matter. Customs duties and tariffs are exclusively federal (Tariff Act of 1930, 19 U.S.C.); U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 10, cl. 2 bars states from laying imposts or duties on imports or exports.

Federal matter. Immigration status and work authorisation are governed by the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C., and I-9 verification by 8 U.S.C. sec. 1324a. South Carolina's adjacent provisions are employer-verification mandates riding on the federal scheme, not work-permit schemes: Title 41, Chapter 8 (Illegal Aliens and Private Employment), Title 8, Chapter 14 (Unauthorized Aliens and Public Employment) and Title 8, Chapter 29 (Verification of Lawful Presence in the United States), all verified in force on the register's own title indexes, with Title 8, Chapter 30 marked [REPEALED].

register.name: South Dakota Legislature - South Dakota Codified Laws (Legislative Research Council)
register.access_notes: Fully accessible. The statute browser is a JavaScript single-page application, so a plain GET of /Statutes/<ref> returns only the app shell; the pages are backed by the Legislature's own public JSON API on the same host, which serves the data the page displays. Endpoint shapes were discovered by loading the site's own pages in a browser and reading the requests the page itself makes, not by guessing or scraping around anything: /api/Statutes/Title lists the 71 Titles, /api/Statutes/Statute/<ref> returns one Title, Chapter or Section, and /api/Statutes/LastStatuesEffectiveDate returns the code's currency date. Requests used the honest user agent 'canon-legislation-indexer/1.0 (legalese/canon corpus metadata survey)' with Accept: application/json; every request returned 200 with no challenge, no rate limiting and no block. The API response carries a Repealed boolean and a CatchLine, which is what in-force status here was taken from, alongside the [Repealed] and [Repealed And Transferred] markers the Title pages print in their chapter index. The API also returns the full statutory text in an Html field: that field was parsed only for chapter names, section numbers and section catchlines and was never copied into this record. About 25 requests in total, spaced 2 s apart. One thing to note honestly: the site's app shell loads Google reCAPTCHA (a site-wide script, presumably for its contact and MyLRC forms); no challenge was ever presented on any statute page or API call, and nothing was bypassed.

licence.summary: Mixed, and the most restrictive of the three verified jurisdictions in this group. The register's own Disclaimer page (https://sdlegislature.gov/Disclaimer) says nothing about copyright or reuse at all - it is a pure accuracy disclaimer. The operative claim is statutory: SDCL 2-16-8 ('Copyrights of material--Contract for use of state's copyright') provides that material in the Codified Laws is copyrighted by the State of South Dakota 'to the extent permitted by federal copyright law', and SDCL 2-16-8.1 makes it a misdemeanour to print or distribute copyrighted material from the Codified Laws except as federal copyright law allows. Both sections were verified in force (Repealed=false) on the register's own API. The qualifier does the work. Under the government edicts doctrine confirmed in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020), statutory text, numbering and section catchlines produced by legislators in their legislative capacity are outside copyright entirely, so federal copyright law permits no state copyright over them; the state's claim can only reach separately authored editorial material, and SDCL 2-16-13.1 in any event excludes editorial material and appendices from the official code. On that reading reuse and adaptation of the statutory text are lawful, and open_licence is set true for the enacted text only. A HUMAN MUST SIGN THIS OFF: unlike South Carolina there is no affirmative permission anywhere, the state asserts copyright by statute, and it attaches a criminal penalty to unauthorised distribution - a materially stronger posture than a bare website footer notice. Note also that the Codified Laws are published in print by a commercial publisher under contract with the Code Commission (SDCL 2-16-7, 2-16-7.1); annotations in that edition are not part of the enacted text and are not covered.
licence.attribution: none stated; good practice is to cite 'South Dakota Codified Laws' with the chapter and the 3 September 2026 effective date, to reproduce only the enacted text rather than any editorial apparatus, and not to present a copy as the official version
licence.quote: The internet version of the South Dakota Codified Laws is made available as a public service. ... In the case of inconsistencies resulting from omissions or other errors, the current printed version of the Code will prevail. [Disclaimer page; the copyright claim itself is statutory - SDCL 2-16-8.1: 'Except as authorized by federal copyright law, no person may print or distribute copyrighted material from the South Dakota Codified Laws']

register.name: Tennessee Code Unannotated - Free Public Access (LexisNexis, published under contract with the Tennessee Code Commission)
register.access_notes: PARTIAL - table-of-contents level only, on a commercial platform, because the State's own register is unreachable. The Tennessee General Assembly's hosts are all refused at the TCP layer from this network: www.capitol.tn.gov (170.142.7.20) and wapp.capitol.tn.gov returned 'connect ECONNREFUSED 170.142.7.20:443' from the agent fetch tool and HTTP code 000 from curl with the honest user agent 'canon-legislation-indexer/1.0 (legalese/canon corpus metadata survey)'; www.tnga.gov and www.tn.gov/sos/acts.html likewise returned 000; sos.tn.gov and publications.tnsosfiles.com returned HTTP 403. The only reachable source for the consolidated Code is the state-sponsored free public access edition that LexisNexis publishes under its contract with the Tennessee Code Commission, at https://www.lexisnexis.com/hottopics/tncode/, which redirects to an advance.lexis.com container. That platform was loaded in an ordinary browser session with no sign-in; NO CAPTCHA and no bot challenge was presented at any point, and nothing was bypassed. WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THIS RECORD: verification for every Act below is TABLE-OF-CONTENTS LEVEL ONLY. The TOC tree was expanded node by node and the exact Title, Chapter, Part and section headings recorded, including the [Reserved] and [Repealed] markers the TOC itself prints; no section text was opened or copied. The platform publishes NO CURRENCY DATE on the table of contents, so no as-at date could be captured, and repeal of an individual section could not be checked beyond what the TOC marks. Two further caveats a human should know: the Lexis page frame is mislabelled 'Georgia General Assembly' in its own header (an apparent template artefact - the source itself is named 'Tennessee Code Table of Contents PAW- ET TABLE OF CONTENTS' and the document title is 'Tennessee Code Unannotated - Free Public Access'), and during one TOC interaction a page script fired a copy handler that wrote to the operating-system clipboard, so the user should check their clipboard before pasting. Justia, FindLaw and Casetext were NOT used. About 20 page interactions, none rapid.

licence.summary: NOT open on the only reachable source. LexisNexis asserts a blanket prohibition over everything on its sites: its copyright page states that no part of the materials may be copied, reproduced, translated or reduced to machine-readable form, in whole or in part, for any reason, and its General Terms and Conditions (effective 5 June 2026) govern use of the Online Services and the Materials in them. That is a platform claim, not a claim the State of Tennessee has made - the Tennessee Code Commission contracts with LexisNexis to publish the Code (T.C.A. secs. 1-1-105 to 1-1-107, verified present in the register's own Title 1 table of contents), and the free public access edition exists because of that contract. As a matter of US law the enacted text itself cannot be owned by anyone: under the government edicts doctrine confirmed in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020) - which was decided against exactly this arrangement, a state code published by a Lexis affiliate under contract with a state code commission - statutory text, numbering and section catchlines produced by legislators in their legislative capacity are outside copyright, and Public.Resource.Org concerned the annotations, not the text. So the text of the Tennessee Code may be reused and adapted; what may not be taken is this publisher's copy of it, its editorial apparatus, its formatting and its platform. open_licence is set false because the only source this network can reach forbids copying on its face. WHAT A HUMAN MUST DO: obtain the Code text from the Tennessee General Assembly's own site (www.capitol.tn.gov), which publishes the Code free of charge, once that host is reachable from a network it does not refuse, and check the notice the General Assembly itself carries there.
licence.attribution: if the Lexis edition is used at all, LexisNexis requires its own copyright notice; for the enacted text taken from the State's own source, cite 'Tennessee Code Annotated' with the title, chapter and part - no attribution is legally required for uncopyrightable statutory text
licence.quote: No part of the materials including graphics or logos, available in this Web site may be copied, photocopied, reproduced, translated or reduced to any electronic medium or machine-readable form, in whole or in part, for any reason.
